title: Tickets, timetables, transportation
topic: buying a ticket, understanding a timetable
why: The start of the unit on travel: you reuse telling time, numbers and the verbs salir and llegar to buy a ticket and understand a timetable at Atocha station or in the Madrid subway. The past tenses you recently learned come back to talk about a missed or delayed train, before the hotel and the imperative in the next lessons.

At the station: buying a ticket

In Spain, people take the train a lot: the AVE (the high-speed train) links Madrid to Seville, Barcelona or Valencia in under three hours, and the cercanías serves the suburbs of the big cities. In Madrid, the main station is called Atocha.

SpanishEnglish
el billete de idathe one-way ticket
el billete de ida y vueltathe round-trip ticket
la taquillathe ticket office
la máquina de billetesthe ticket machine
el asientothe seat
ventanilla / pasillowindow / aisle
el andénthe platform
la víathe track

At the ticket office

Buenos días. Quería un billete de ida y vuelta para Sevilla.Good morning. I'd like a round-trip ticket to Seville.
¿Para qué día? — Para el viernes, por la mañana.For what day? — For Friday, in the morning.
¿Ventanilla o pasillo? — Ventanilla, por favor.Window or aisle? — Window, please.

You recognize the polite phrase quería (I'd like): it's the imperfect of querer, which you now know how to conjugate. You say a ticket para Sevilla (the destination) or a Sevilla: both are correct.

El billete means both “the train ticket” and “the bill” (banknote). In Latin America, a train ticket is often el boleto or el pasaje.

", "

Understanding a timetable

For timetables, the present is enough, as in English (el tren sale a las ocho, the train leaves at eight). Two verbs do all the work: salir (to leave) and llegar (to arrive).

TrenSalida (Madrid-Atocha)Llegada (Sevilla)Vía
AVE 208008:0010:305
AVE 210010:0012:383
AVE 212012:0514:457
¿A qué hora sale el próximo tren para Sevilla? — Sale a las diez y llega a las doce y treinta y ocho.What time does the next train to Seville leave? — It leaves at ten and arrives at twelve thirty-eight.
¿De qué vía sale? — De la vía tres.What track does it leave from? — From track three.

Timetable words

  • la salida = departure; la llegada = arrival (careful, la salida also means “the exit”).
  • puntual = on time; con retraso = late, delayed: El tren llega con diez minutos de retraso.
  • directo = direct; hacer transbordo = to change trains, to make a connection.
  • ¿Cuánto dura el viaje? = How long is the trip?

In stations and announcements, times are given on the 24-hour clock: a las catorce treinta (14:30, 2:30 p.m.). In conversation, people quickly go back to a las dos y media.

", "

In town: the subway and the cercanías

The Madrid subway (the metro) is big and easy to use. The lines have a number and a color, and people say la línea 1, la línea 3. To travel, you top up a tarjeta de transporte (transit card).

SpanishEnglishExample
coger el metroto take the subwayCojo el metro todos los días.
la líneathe line¿La línea 1 va a Sol?
la parada / la estaciónthe stop / the stationMe bajo en la tercera parada.
bajarseto get off¿Dónde te bajas?
subir al trento get on the trainSubimos al tren a las ocho.
cambiar de líneato change linesEn Sol cambias a la línea 3.
recargar la tarjetato top up the cardQuería recargar la tarjeta.
Para ir al Museo del Prado, coges la línea 1 hasta Estación del Arte y te bajas allí.To get to the Prado Museum, you take line 1 to Estación del Arte and get off there.

To give a route, Spanish uses the present, as you already did for giving walking directions: coges, cambias, te bajas.

In Spain, coger is the normal verb for “taking” a means of transportation. In several Latin American countries, people prefer tomar (tomar el bus), because coger has a vulgar meaning there.
